title: Helius Sjamsuddin and Suhartono W. Pranoto in Indonesian Historical Methodology
abstract: This article examines how Helius Sjamsuddin and Suhartono W. Pranoto conceptualized historical methodology in comparison with the methodological legacy of Sartono Kartodirdjo and Kuntowijoyo. Kartodirdjo’s pioneering contribution lay in distinguishing historical methodology from historical method and in developing a multidimensional social-science approach rooted in the first National History Seminar and his dissertation research. Using the historical method (heuristics, criticism, interpretation, and historiography), this study treats Sjamsuddin’s Metodologi Sejarah (2007) and Pranoto’s Teori & Metodologi Sejarah (2010) as intellectual-history sources. The findings show that both works combine historical method and historical methodology within single reference books, thereby obscuring the distinction between practical research procedures and theoretical reflection. Although both historians contributed to the teaching of historical studies, their works give limited attention to historical theories, concepts, and approaches derived from auxiliary sciences. This article argues for a clearer separation between historical method as practice and historical methodology as theory.

title: TWO ACCOUNTS OF HISTORICAL KNOWLEDGE: HISTORIOGRAPHIC REASONING AND NARRATIVE ACCORDING TO AVIEZER TUCKER AND CHIEL VAN DEN AKKER1
abstract: ABSTRACT This review essay examines a recurring distinction in the philosophy of history between the phase of establishing historical facts or knowledge claims and the phase of interpreting them. Focusing on two recent books by Aviezer Tucker and Chiel van den Akker, it analyzes how each author conceptualizes historical knowledge by emphasizing one of these phases. Tucker locates the core of historical practice in evidential reasoning and the production of knowledge claims about past events, which he regards as the basis for consensus among historians. In contrast, van den Akker concentrates on the construction and understanding of narrative theses and argues that historical narratives are not direct descriptions of evidence but unique interpretations. This review essay argues that, although the distinction between research and interpretation can be somewhat useful, an attempt to synthesize Tucker's and van den Akker's accounts into a single and more comprehensive theory of historical knowledge would be problematic. Since each framework highlights one phase and leaves the other underdeveloped, a meaningful theory of historical work must be developed internally within one conceptual framework rather than assembled from incompatible accounts with distinct priorities.

title: Representations of precolonial androgyny and the figure of Tipu Sultan in Gidwani and Karnad
abstract: This article re-examines Tipu Sultan beyond colonial and nationalist representations that hyper-masculinize him as either predatory or benevolent. I use the term hyper-masculinization to describe a representational stratagem in which Indian rulers are depicted in lopsided extremes: either as excessively violent and aggressive or conversely as overly compassionate and weak. Such single-dimensional representations sideline the wider cultural meanings of masculinity associated with the traditional Indian conception of androgyny. This study fills this gap by arguing that Tipu’s personality is far more profound and many sided and can be better apprehended through the hitherto overlooked conception of androgyny, understood in Ashis Nandy’s work as a marker of masculinity in pre-colonial India. Here androgyny is not a form of gender ambiguity but a culturally bounded ideal of balance that sacralizes political agency, controlled violence, and creativity. Drawing on Ashis Nandy’s conceptualization of Indian masculinity as well as Hindu and Islamic metaphysical worldviews, I argue that Indian fictional writings such as Girish Karnad’s The Dreams of Tipu Sultan and Bhawan S. Gidwani’s The Sword of Tipu Sultan can be read as presenting Tipu as an androgynous sovereign. In doing so, these texts stand in sharp contrast to the colonial demonization and nationalist romanticization of Tipu as a hypermasculine individual. While neither Karnad nor Gidwani may have explicitly set out to recover …

title: Getting by but not getting ahead: Muslim families, community networks, and school lunch accommodations in Kumamoto City, Japan
abstract: As Japan’s Muslim population grows, religious accommodation in public schooling is increasingly pressing, yet existing research has focused on individual families and schools while overlooking Muslim community networks. This study examines why Muslim families in Kumamoto City are ‘getting by’ in securing school lunch accommodations but not ‘getting ahead’: why, despite an organised community centred around the Kumamoto Islamic Centre (KIC), parents continue negotiating individually rather than collectively. Drawing on interviews with Muslim parents and Japanese educators, the study employs a social capital framework distinguishing bonding, bridging, and linking capital. Families rely on co-ethnic bonding networks. Bridging capital within KIC has not been mobilised around halal because diversity of interpretation prevents a collective position from forming; without it, linking capital connecting the community to schools and authorities cannot develop. Three accommodation types are documented: an informal parent-led arrangement, a formalised shared-responsibility system (the ABCD system), and an institution-led full provision model. The ABCD system has the greatest potential for broader application. The study argues that the absence of a unified community position is a structural feature of how halal is practised in a diverse community, and that systemic improvement requires municipal frameworks that support school-level accommodation without presupposing collective consensus.

title: Bad fakes and the concept of success
abstract: This article explores the concept of a successful, or convincing, forgery. What makes a forgery successful and why? Drawing from a range of high-profile and lesser-known cases of forgery from the eighteenth to twenty-first centuries, this article examines the dominant notions of success in forgery and challenges the assumptions that uphold them. It demonstrates that although the conditions that enable the creation of a successful forgery are multifaceted and vary considerably, what exactly constitutes a successful forgery is inextricably linked with its capacity to deceive. However, by decentring the importance of deception in the makings of a successful forgery, this article makes space for thinking about the bad, childish fakes that occupy the lower ends of the antiquities market in particular as successful and in what capacity. It concludes by arguing that bad fakes, much like bad art or bad movies, can simultaneously embody multiple and at times radically divergent notions of success unrelated to their ability (or inability) to deceive.

title: The present state of Japanese research on the Chinese Communist Party: report on the joint review workshop “Great Dissection of the CCP”
abstract: Abstract The present article focuses on five recent Japanese-language research monographs on the history of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), authored respectively by Eda Kenji, Mishina Hidenori, Zhou Jun, Takahashi Nobuo, and Suzuki Takashi. The books cover a wide span, reaching from the history of the early years of the CCP through the Communist-Nationalist civil war era, the early years after the founding of the People’s Republic, the implementation of the Great Leap Forward policy, the Cultural Revolution, and until the contemporary Xi Jinping regime. Based on a joint review workshop held at the Institute for Research in the Humanities at Kyoto University in 2025, the article discusses the contributions of the five books and the perspectives of their respective reviewers.

title: A French revolutionary political club and its global contexts: The Society of Lorient, 1790–94
abstract: Abstract How can a political society established in one port city in Revolutionary France be a ‘global’ actor? This article examines the revolutionary Society of Lorient, an Atlantic port founded to be the seat of the French East India Company, as a case study of the viability of the ‘micro-spatial’ approach to global history outlined by Christian De Vito. It considers how the Lorient Society positioned itself as an intermediary between global concerns and the French national authorities, as well as the Society’s evolving perspective on global imperial rivalries in their relationship to revolution, the ‘rights of man’, trade, war, race, and slavery. In doing so, it shows how a seemingly local actor could help construct the global in the context of the ‘Age of Revolution(s)’ of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

title: The Historiosophical Views of A.I. Denikin
abstract: This article analyzes the historiosophical views of General A.I. Denikin, as expressed in his “Essays on the Russian Time of Troubles”. The author explores Denikin's belief that history is called upon to reveal the underlying causes of political catastrophes, rooted in the country's past and the spirit of the people. His skepticism regarding the possibility of attaining “absolute truth” and his recognition of the inevitable subjectivity of historical evidence are emphasized. Particular attention is given to Denikin's religious, apophatic worldview, according to which history merely reflects “reflections” of a higher truth. In conclusion, it is noted that his historiosophical position, despite its integrity, is limited by his lack of a systematic historical education.
journal: Herald of Omsk University Series Historical Studies

title: Wartime Historian V.N. Bernadsky: Intellectual Heritage and Dissertation Narrative
abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of the intellectual heritage of historian Viktor Nikolaevich Bernadsky, an honored teacher and specialist in the history of Novgorod. During the Great Patriotic War, Bernadsky, being evacuated to the Urals, builds a regional military-historical narrative, following the official patriotic course. Using the example of analyzing the texts of candidate's and doctoral dissertations, the author of the article shows how wartime determined the evolution of the scientist's views.

Companion Animal Clinic as a Medium: Emergence and Development of Veterinary Professional Modernity in China
abstract: Abstract Few studies investigate the relationship between veterinary practices and companion animals in China considering its social development and the historical transformation of the veterinary profession. This study examines the historical changes in the development of the veterinary profession in China between 1985 and 1995, using the Companion Animal Clinic ( CAC , 伴侣动物门诊部 ) of Beijing Agricultural University ( BAU ) as a case study. Through a theoretical thematic analysis of oral history and interview data, results show that the CAC played a spatial medium role in the emergence of the modern veterinary professional identity in China. The veterinary practices and social structures which differed from those of the Mao era, along with the structural duality between them, served as a key driving force in the ongoing development of the modern veterinary profession. The study fills a gap in the literature and highlights trends that require ongoing support.

title: The Tokyo Shichū Ongakukai: commercial bands and the informal spread of Western music in Meiji Japan
abstract: The adoption and spread of Western music in Meiji-era Japan (1868–1912) is often explained through formal, state-led initiatives such as military bands, educational reforms, and the establishment of institutions including the Tokyo Academy of Music. While these state initiatives created the infrastructure for musical change, they do not fully explain how Western music eventually came to be heard and enjoyed by the broader public. This article examines the role of commercially organised wind and brass ensembles in the informal diffusion of Western music during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It centres on the Tokyo Shichū Ongakukai (Tokyo City Band), a privately organised band founded in 1887 that transformed military musical practices into entrepreneurial entertainment, giving performances at hotels, parks, and other urban venues in and around Yokohama. Drawing on a micro-historical reading of a 1942 interview with co-founder Ikeda Tatsugorō, the article reconstructs the everyday experiences of musicians navigating the emerging commercial and cosmopolitan worlds of Meiji Japan. Situating the band alongside related phenomena such as department store youth bands and mobile street ensembles known as jinta, the study argues that Western music spread not only through state institutions but also through commercial spectacle and consumer culture.

title: A new exploration of Zheng Xuan’s Confucian classics studies and thoughts based on machine learning analysis of “Zheng Zhi”
abstract: Abstract Zheng Zhi (⟪鄭志⟫) records the dialogs between Zheng Xuan (鄭玄) and his disciples and is a key source for late Eastern Han Confucianism. Its surviving fragments are scattered and transmission-biased, and existing scholarship has focused on textual recovery rather than systematic analysis of Zheng Xuan’s intellectual architecture. Two unresolved problems underlie this scholarship: the fragmentation of Zheng Xuan studies into isolated domains, and the widely accepted but potentially reductive characterization of his scholarship as organized around Rites of Zhou (⟪周禮⟫) alone. This study proposes two analytically distinct dimensions for understanding Zheng Xuan’s classical system. The classical dimension identifies a Classic of Poetry (⟪詩經⟫)–Rites of Zhou dual-center structure at the chapter level of Zheng Zhi, challenging the single-center model. The conceptual dimension reveals a deeper binary framework of fa (institution, 法) and ji (history, 迹). Fa—“Duke of Zhou’s (周公) method for achieving great peace”—is the normative system of governance; ji—“Duke of Zhou’s deeds in achieving great peace”—is the empirical record of how institutions were realized across dynasties. On the surface, fa and ji are a distinction among classical texts; at the deeper conceptual level, they constitute an integrated historical philosophy of “varying institutions of successive dynasties.” Within this framework, Zheng Xuan’s “li” (ritual, 禮) undergoes a fundamental transformation from ritual …

title: Affective polarization and the politics of visibility: Digital diffusion of the Takae anti-base protests in Okinawa
abstract: This study explores how digital communication shaped the visibility and emotional dynamics of the 2016 anti-U.S. base protest in Takae, Okinawa. Using Japanese-language Twitter (now X) data, it analyzes how structural resources, message characteristics, and emotions influenced political diffusion across polarized communities. To capture both entry into diffusion and large-scale amplification, the study combines hurdle models with quantile regression. The findings reveal a two-stage process of online diffusion. At the entry stage, visibility is driven primarily by structural resources such as the follower size and favorites. At higher levels of diffusion, however, affective and semantic dynamics become more important. In the anti-base movement Support community, anger facilitates high-end diffusion, whereas in the anti-protest Opposition community, disgust becomes a major driver of virality. Hashtags do not consistently amplify diffusion, while tweets containing external links become less likely to spread widely, particularly among opponents. The analysis further shows how Twitter connected Okinawa with mainland Japan through influencer-centered circulation, increasing national visibility while simultaneously intensifying political polarization. These findings suggest that online visibility is not distributed evenly across digital publics but structured by asymmetries in attention, affect, and communicative influence. The case of Takae therefore illustrates how digital …

title: Bridging migration and arrival: Foreigner-friendly real estate agencies and migrant housing access in Japan
abstract: This paper examines the practices of foreigner-friendly real estate agencies in Japan and their role in shaping foreign migrants’ access to the rental housing market and early settlement experiences. Despite Japan’s increasing reliance on foreign labor, access to rental housing remains structurally constrained for non-Japanese due to discrimination, guarantor requirements, language barriers, and limited institutional support. Drawing on qualitative interviews, with real estate agents providing services to Vietnamese migrants in Japan and with foreign migrants, as well as ethnographic observations conducted in Tokyo and social media, the paper analyzes how real estate agencies as market actors have developed business strategies tailored to foreign migrants in response to Japan’s changing immigration landscape and expanding foreign population. It shows that these agencies mediate housing access by matching migrant profiles with suitable local properties, arranging viewings, and brokering administrative, bureaucratic, and legal services, thereby shaping migrants’ post-arrival experiences. Empirical data suggest that foreigner-friendly real estate agencies are an active actor within the arrival infrastructure that facilitates migrants’ settlement in Japan. At the same time, their transnational collaboration with other migration brokers overseas positions these agencies within the migration infrastructure that influences mobility pathways and trajectories. Highlighting the …

title: Thresholds of meaning: metaphor, conceptual change and historical imagination
abstract: This essay analyzes the structuring role of metaphors in contemporary historiography by engaging in dialogue with three key works: Key Metaphors for History by Javier Fernández Sebastián, Intellectual History and the Problem of Conceptual Change by Elías José Palti and History and Identity by Stefan Berger. Across three sections, it reconstructs the convergences among these proposals concerning the epistemic function of metaphors, understood not as stylistic embellishments but as figurative matrices that mediate between experience, language and historical interpretation. First, it examines how metaphors shape forms of historical reasoning and grammars of temporality. Second, it analyzes their role as catalysts of conceptual change, particularly in contexts of semantic crisis or epistemic dislocation. Finally, it explores the potential of a historical metaphorology to foster interdisciplinary dialogue among history, philosophy, political theory, visual studies and material culture. What is thus advocated is a critical renewal of historical theory – one capable of training historians who are aware of the tropological substratum of their practice and equipped with tools to intervene in public debates on memory, identity and the uses of the past. Metaphors, in this framework, not only serve to weave historical narratives, but they also make them possible.

title: Историческое сознание населения Казахстана (по материалам экспертного опроса 2021 г.): Научная статья
abstract: The article presents the results of sociological research conducted within the framework of the project “Development of scientifically grounded concept of formation of modern historical science of Kazakhstan”. One hundred Kazakhstani experts-historians specializing in various aspects of the development of domestic historical science were surveyed by means of in-depth interviews and questionnaire methods. Historiographical analysis of works of Kazakhstani and foreign scientists determined that conducting sociological surveys in Kazakhstan in the field of history is a very rare phenomenon. They were mainly related to the study of the state of historical consciousness. The conducted survey addressed the problem of formation and the state of historical memory of modern Kazakhstanis, as it was assessed by the experts themselves. The issues studied included attitude and interest in history, the level of historical literacy, and many others. An important issue was the opinion of experts on the demand of the scientific community to create a new concept of historical consciousness to replace the one that was adopted in the mid-1990s. Another significant part of this study was to identify the most effective, in the opinion of experts, tools for the formation of historical memory: cinema, books, mass media, school, etc., as well as to assess their role and degree of influence. A survey conducted among Kazakhstani experts–professional historians–allowed us to draw a number of …
journal: Journal of the National Congress of Historians

title: Charting the shattered sea: Maritime geopolitics and transnational oceanography in East Asia, 1984–2007
abstract: Abstract This article examines the challenges of border-crossing science at geopolitical hot spots through the case study of the East Sea (also known as the Sea of Japan). The East Sea is a marginal sea on the north-west Pacific Ocean surrounded by four historically conflicted nations—South Korea, North Korea, Russia, and Japan. Despite vast scientific interest, severe military conflicts have restricted transnational cooperation in this region throughout the late twentieth century. Utilizing personal archives, cruise reports, and interviews with participating scientists, this article examines how an international team of East Asian oceanographers developed material, political, and rhetorical tactics to circumvent and even appropriate complex border problems at the end of the Cold War. The case study suggests that the global history of oceanography should pay further attention to the practical challenges of accessing geopolitically conflicted basins as well as creative strategies that scientists devise to bridge over those troubled waters.

title: Faith, Famine, and Resilience: The 1817 Subsistence Crisis during the Megadrought in Catalonia
abstract: The article analyses the social consequences of the subsistence crisis and water scarcity in 1817, one of the most severe years of the megadrought (1812–1824) that affected northeastern Spain. Drawing on municipal records from Barcelona, Tarragona and Girona, ecclesiastical documentation and commercial correspondence from a grain trading company, it examines how hydrological stress disrupted food supply, intensified conflicts over water access and shaped relations between rural communities and urban authorities. Harvest failure contributed to rising grain prices and increased migration in a post-war context marked by institutional fragility. In response, authorities and local institutions promoted charitable initiatives, public works and regulatory measures to secure water and grain supplies. Evidence from Urgell, an agricultural region of Catalonia, illustrates the scale of agricultural losses and peasant displacement. The study conceptualises drought as a socially embedded crisis shaped by prolonged environmental stress, governance constraints and unequal resource access.

title: Engineering Redemption: Francoist Colonisation Villages and the Making of Spain’s Fascist Landscape
abstract: This article situates Francoist colonisation villages within broader debates about nature and nation in twentieth-century fascist regimes. It argues that the Franco regime’s ambitious hydraulic program – dams and irrigation networks – must be understood both as a material reconfiguration of territory and as an authoritarian strategy for reorganising rural populations. Through the coordination of hydraulic engineering, agricultural planning and settlement construction, the Instituto Nacional de Colonización y Desarrollo Rural (National Institute of Colonisation) consolidated a new irrigated agrarian order while reinforcing existing landholding structures and producing technically trained, politically loyal subjects. Alongside these material interventions, newsreels played a crucial role in shaping the meanings attached to this transformed national nature, framing the domestication of water and territory as a providential project of national regeneration and representing colonisation villages as idealised rural communities. By analysing their cinematic representation, this article highlights the importance of visual construction in naturalising authoritarian modernisation while obscuring social conflict and ecological disruption. Colonisation villages thus emerge as key nodes in the fusion of hydraulic modernisation, political control and national mythmaking.

title: Pre-revolution network connections of the 1989 Polish Round Table participants
abstract: Between the late 1940s and the collapse of Communism in 1989, the Polish United Workers Party (PZPR) controlled nearly all facets of political and social life in Poland. Communist rule was contested regularly, however, with a spontaneous worker uprising in Pozńan in 1956, a national student uprising in 1968, worker strikes in Gdańsk in 1970 and outside of Warsaw in 1976. These earlier uprisings were precursors to the strikes along the Baltic Coast that led to the creation of the independent, self-governing Trade Union "Solidarity" in August 1980. Solidarity was forced into the underground by a declaration of martial law in December 1981 but rebuilt itself as a broad-based social movement during the 1980s. When another round of strikes occurred in 1988, the Communist government turned to Solidarity to find a political solution to Poland’s endemic instability and the two groups joined Round Table meetings in early 1989. These negotiations resulted in a peaceful transition to a Democratic government later that year, the first revolution in a cascade of anti-Communist revolutions that swept the region in 1989/1990. Using a dataset of the institutional affiliations of the 567 Round Table participants, a purpose-built Shiny App for longitudinally analyzing the dataset, and a penalized logistic model, this paper shows that while the creation of the Solidarity Trade Union in August 1980 was the most transformational moment for the network structure that linked Round Table …

title: Constructing a Colonial State: The Land Rights Debate in Eighteenth-Century Bengal
abstract: Abstract The paper reinterprets the East India Company’s state-building effort in late eighteenth‑century Bengal by foregrounding the intertwined evolution of fiscal capacity and institutional reform. It argues that the Permanent Settlement of 1793 emerged not from a desire to follow Indian or English precedent, but from the Company’s struggle to concentrate fiscal powers. A debate on the need to obtain information on taxpayers, which delayed the reform, reveals this struggle. Repeated failures in data collection pushed the state to anchor the reform in an expanding judicial system capable of producing actionable information. The Settlement strengthened revenue flows, enabling the financing of a centrally controlled army and contributing to Britain’s wider imperial expansion. However, its long-term rigidity limited fiscal flexibility and impeded broader developmental outcomes.
journal: Comparative Studies in Society and History

title: The Aesthetics of Photographic Production
abstract: The Aesthetics of Photographic Production is a media-rich Research Catalogue exposition emerging from an AHRC-funded long-term practice research project (2018–24) that investigates photographic production as a multisensory, material, and more-than-human field of making. The project’s dissemination strategy is threefold: this exposition, a published monograph (Jaeger 2025), and the performance and exhibition of artworks, each calibrated to communicate the research through distinct epistemic affordances. Grounded in sensory field encounters within commercial laboratories and manufacturing facilities — Bayeux London, Make it Easy Lab Nottingham, Fujifilm Tilburg, and Polaroid Enschede — the exposition foregrounds production ecologies where photographic work emerges through distributed relations among technicians, machines, paper, chemistry, protocols, speed, and darkness.The exposition is organised by two objectives: to examine what else besides the photograph is aesthetically made in photographic production, and to explore the implications of this shift for the concept of photographic practice (Jaeger 2025). These aims are pursued through four subpages — tensioning, tearing, fogging, and fieldwork — which assemble visual, sonic, and audiovisual materials to render process insights encounterable. Rather than privileging the finished image, the exposition attends to practices of calibration, residue, and non-image making, where touch, listening, rhythm, and material agency …

title: Editorial Foreword
abstract: This issue brings together nine research articles grouped under four rubrics, spanning topics that range from imperial legacies in Spain and Iran to the politics of racialization across micro and macro scales, as well as frontier politics and the histories of possession and dispossession in the Ottoman world. IMPERIAL TRANSLATIONSIn "Epistemic Translation of Modernity: Negotiating Science and Technology under Semi-Colonial Conditions," Mina Khanlarzadeh turns to the vexed question of semi-colonial sovereignty and specifically how Iranian intellectuals negotiated Western science and technology through creative acts of translation.Translation was not simply linguistic transfer but a set of practices ranging from adoption to refusal that shaped this unequal encounter, whose legacies play themselves out in particularly visible and devastating fashion in this historical juncture.Yves Winter's essay is equally a study in imperial translations, violence, and erasures.In "Imperial Nostalgia as Patrimony: Shipwrecks and Treasures in the Colonial Museum," Winter highlights how two recent Spanish museum exhibitions on the frigate Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes convert recovered colonial treasure into objects of national patrimony.Through a reading of the exhibits and the media and academic discourse around them, the essay emphasizes the ways that these displays translate and transform imperial histories into national heritage while bracketing questions of extraction, coercion, and …

title: Decontesting Historical Consciousness
abstract: Decontesting Historical Consciousness provides a comprehensive exploration of historical consciousness, redefining it not just as an academic concept but as a fundamental human state of mind essential for navigating the modern world. By approaching historical consciousness from an ontological perspective and by viewing humans and the world as both “history-made” and “history-making,” the text illuminates how our understanding of the past directly shapes our individual well-being and collective survival. After an overview of how historical consciousness has been defined over time, this book offers a new ontological definition of the concept. Then it proceeds to analyse the historicity of the world and the human, the historicity of time and historical narratives, and the ways in which history is used. Furthermore, the book discusses the relation of historical consciousness to historical knowledge and historical thinking. A distinctive feature of the work is the introduction of original typologies, including an 11-part model of historical thinking and a three-tiered quality level of consciousness: Innate, reflective, and scholarly. The author also bridges the gap between theory and practice by examining the application of history in politics, education, and entertainment, while utilizing Bloom’s taxonomy to categorize historical knowledge. Designed for scholars, students, and practitioners in history, history education, philosophy, and sociology, this book is an essential …

title: On the 95th anniversary of I. Kh. Kadyrov
abstract: Kadyrov Ilgiz Khanovich (1931–2013) was a historian, an educator, and a public figure. Born in the village of Novye Chelny, the Alkeyevsky District in the Tatar ASSR, he graduated from the History Department of the Kazan State Pedagogical Institute (1949–1953) and completed his postgraduate studies at the Moscow State Pedagogical Institute named after V. I. Lenin (1964–1967). He received the degree of сandidate of history (1971) and was a secretary of the Komsomol Committee of the Kazan State Pedagogical Institute (1954–1960). First, he worked as assistant (1954), then, as associate professor (1973) in the Department of General History at the Kazan State Pedagogical Institute. From 1988 to 2008, he was Head of the Department of General History at the Kazan State Pedagogical Institute. Ilgiz Kadyrov was the author of works on modern history of Asian and African countries and the works on the content and methods of teaching history at universities. He was awarded an Honorary Diploma of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the Tatar ASSR (1958) and Honorary Diplomas of the Tatar Regional Committee of the CPSU and the Council of Ministers of the Tatar ASSR. In 1992, he got the title of an Honored Cultural Worker of the Republic of Tatarstan.

title: Narrating modern crisis and acceleration: re-reading Carl Schorske’s Fin de Siècle Vienna
abstract: In the late nineteenth century, the economic, social and cultural accelerations of western modernity triggered intensifying reactions, including racism, nationalism and communitarian politics, that sought refuge in tradition from the threat of change. Conversely, cultural movements emerged that embraced the dynamics of innovation. Carl Schorske’s Fin de Siècle Vienna: Politics and Culture, immersed in the complexity of these contesting responses enacted in a critical cultural and intellectual milieu of the period. Schorske sought resolution of fin de siècle crisis and acceleration through catharsis, presenting at least the possibility of a restoration of cultural unity; yet his narrative more convincingly described forces of disintegration generated by the drive for progress. Drawing on the work of Reinhart Koselleck and the debate on modern crisis and acceleration stimulated by it, Schorske’s seminal work is explored to develop a reconsideration of the intellectual and cultural energies generating progress and crisis at the fin de siècle and resonating into the twentieth century.

title: Futures in the present: Food allergy disclosures at work
abstract: Food and work are often inextricably linked in Japan. However, for those with multiple food allergies, such expectations can be difficult to navigate. Drawing on fieldwork with young adults since 2017, this article explores how they experience workplace expectations to eat and drink together, and the different strategies they use to negotiate eating with others as they move from student life to being a shakaijin (social adult). For people with experience of severe food allergies, the potential of a negative future is ever-present in the guise of the possibility of experiencing a severe allergic reaction. However, because food is strongly implicated in the building and maintenance of social relations, avoiding food can create social risks. These risks are heightened when food sharing is a feature of workplace relations, both within and between companies. Gaining a negative reputation for being difficult because of not sharing food or joining workplace events can have potential consequences on promotion and is also a future to avoid. I argue that imagined futures are ever-present in allergy disclosures, and it is disclosure itself which operates as a juncture in which potential futures that exist in individuals' present – through their imagination – are used to open different possible futures in life and at work. This article consequently explores the important, but often overlooked, influence of food on workplace relationships and how the labour of disclosure contributes to …

title: Visions in the Machine: Automated Tagging of the William Blake Archive
abstract: This paper investigates how multimodal AI can support — not replace — scholarly description of William Blake’s visual art. Using the William Blake Archive as a foundation, I develop a conceptual framework that distinguishes three levels of visual analysis (pattern recognition, motif identification, and iconographic interpretation) and use it to evaluate a working retrieval prototype built on Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) embeddings and Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) indexing over a 200-work stratified corpus. The paper defends three claims. First, that AI-assisted tagging is best understood as retrieval support rather than automated interpretation: it surfaces candidate matches that scholars then validate. Second, that performance degrades predictably across the three tiers: strong at object-level detection, moderate at motif-level pattern recognition, weak at Blake-specific iconography, and that this gradient is itself a useful empirical finding for archives weighing adoption. Third, that the responsible integration of AI tags into an existing scholarly archive requires explicit provenance, confidence scoring, human-in-the-loop validation, and audit logging, and that these requirements can be operationalized concretely. The paper does not claim to automate iconographic interpretation, to provide ground-truth identifications, or to generalize beyond the 200-work pilot; results should be read as alignment with the Archive’s descriptive practice on a …

title: Unruly Singing and Shouting: Listening to Labourers’ Work Songs in Modern Shanghai
abstract: Abstract As early as the third century bce, references to labourers’ work songs appeared in the Chinese court-sponsored compendium Lushi Chunqiu, and, for the 2,000 years that followed, labourers throughout China continued to sing these songs. Despite variations in their tones, rhythms, and lyrics, their chanting performed some essential functions: synchronizing movements, communicating information, and boosting morale. During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, however, the sound of such songs became controversial among newly arrived Anglophone settlers as well as Chinese intellectuals in Shanghai, evoking emotions ranging from frustration, contempt, and desperation to compassion, admiration, and even inspiration. This article historicizes the contested interpretations of Chinese workers’ singing and shouting, exploring how different listeners’ anxieties and agendas shaped what they heard. At the same time, it juxtaposes these reactions with the labourers’ own justifications for the sounds they made, and their responses to the baffling modern cityscape they had to navigate. While reconstructing the histories of marginalized groups has long been hindered by the perception of archival silence, attending to sonic traces often dismissed as ‘mere noise’ can help to recover the vital sounds of those otherwise rendered voiceless by the historical record.

title: The Early Islamic Conquests Database–Balādhurī (EICD-B): large language model extraction of conquest data from Futūḥ al-buldān
abstract: Abstract This article introduces the Early Islamic Conquests Database–Balādhurī (EICD-B), a structured dataset extracted from al-Balādhurī’s ninth-century chronicle Futūḥ al-buldān using large language models (LLMs). Building on the OpenITI/KITAB digital corpus, a four-stage workflow transforms narrative historical material into machine-readable conquest records: pre-processing, schema-guided extraction, normalization, and validation. Each record contains the Hijrī year, toponym, commander name, caliph name, and mode of conquest (Capitulation/ṣulḥan, Subjugation/ʿanwatan, or Reconsolidation), with a textual evidence snippet enabling source verification. The validated dataset comprises 226 conquest events dated primarily to 11–97 AH (632–716 CE), with three events (99 and 221 AH) retained as temporal outliers, all successfully geocoded. Results indicate 52.2% Capitulation, 42.5% Subjugation, and 5.3% Reconsolidation. ʿUmar’s caliphate dominates with 99 conquests (43.8%), while fitna periods show a marked decline in conquest activity. EICD-B provides the first machine-readable, evidence-linked dataset of early Islamic conquest events extracted from a classical Arabic chronicle, enabling quantitative testing of historiographical hypotheses such as Noth’s schemata thesis. The study demonstrates a replicable LLM-based workflow for schema-guided extraction from historically inflected Arabic, while emphasizing the methodological importance of retaining textual evidence spans for …

title: ENSINANDO SOBRE O PASSADO DO PARQUE NACIONAL SERRA DA CAPIVARA (PIAUÍ-BRASIL): UMA ANÁLISE APLICADA AO ENSINO BÁSICO ATRAVÉS DO CONTEÚDO DE LIVROS DIDÁTICOS
abstract: O Parque Nacional Serra da Capivara (PI) é uma referência no que se refere àquestões de preservação cultural e ambiental, tanto no Brasil quanto ao nivelinternacional. Dada sua importância para a sociedade, torna-se relevanteinvestigar a sua relação com a educação, e como isso pode ser abordadonos espaços formais e não formais de ensino. O presente trabalho tem comoobjetivo elaborar uma proposta de ‘reconstrução’ do passado do P. N. Serrada Capivara, com base numa investigação dos conteúdos relacionadosa este tema presentes em livros didáticos, visando a aplicação no ensinobásico. Entre os principais aspectos considerados para esta análise, sãodestacados a história da região em análise, a estrutura do currículo regional,as características da didática relacionadas ao conteúdo abordado nos livros.Em termos metodológicos, esta investigação esteve baseada em revisão dabibliografi a disponível, combinado a realização de entrevistas com pessoasdas áreas escolhidas para o estudo aplicado (as cidades piauienses deCoronel José Dias e São Raimundo Nonato). Através desta pesquisa foi possívelcompreender a situação atual da educação na região de infl uencia do P. N.Serra da Capivara e a sua relação com a comunidade, sendo destacadocomo a população local se identifi ca com o bem patrimonial e como o mesmoé capaz de gerar valores e sentidos. Ressalta-se a importancia deste últimoaspecto, com vistas a impulsionar cada vez mais a valorização da experiênciacom a educação patrimonial através …

title: Making history enjoyable: rules and resonance in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms video game series
abstract: This article examines how the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (RTK) video game series transforms history into a source of gameplay enjoyment. Moving beyond debates over historical accuracy and authenticity, it asks how history functions for video games rather than how video games serve history. The article analyzes RTK through two interconnected dimensions: the rule-based reconfiguration of historical materials and resonance between the game and players, understood as a twofold mechanism for generating enjoyment. The article argues that RTK reorganizes historiographical records, literary narratives, and modern media representations into a calculable game system structured through quantified character attributes, turn-based temporality, restricted historical agency, and conquest-oriented goals. Through these rule structures, historical complexity is translated into a framework that enables prediction, planning, and strategic decision-making. The gameplay experience is further recontextualized through resonance, as players relate emergent in-game narratives to their prior knowledge of the Three Kingdoms. By foregrounding the interplay between systemic abstraction, which constructs a generalized rule-based framework, and resonance, which reconfigures gameplay through individualized meaning-making, this article argues that historical video games do not simply represent the past but generate historically grounded enjoyment through the interaction among rules, players, and …

title: Spatiotemporal analysis of local elite groups across generations in Zhejiang, China
abstract: Abstract The relationship between local elite groups and regional cultural evolution across temporal and spatial dimensions has long been critical for understanding how civilizations change. This study employed interdisciplinary methodologies from digital humanities and historical geography to conduct an empirical analysis of 32,207 biographies recorded in local chronicles from the Zhejiang region, spanning the Eastern Zhou Dynasty to the modern era (i.e., 770 BCE–1945 CE). The social composition, achievements, spatial concentration, and diffusion patterns of local elites within the context of different historical periods were of particular interest, alongside their interactions with regional cultural development. It was found that the diversification of local elite types in the Zhejiang region was pronounced, with distinct temporal characteristics, encompassing roles in science and education, politics, literature and art, and medicine. Elites in the field of science and education had the highest probability distribution, accounting for 30.8 per cent, while those in medicine and the military had the lowest, at 13.6 per cent and 12.2 per cent, respectively. The criteria for selecting and recording elite figures changed over time but consistently reflected the trajectory of alterations in mainstream societal values. The importance of cultural heritage and regional characteristics was particularly evident for literature and the arts but was less apparent in science, technology, …

title: The Fuji TV scandal: From sexual assault to corporate disaster
abstract: This article examines the 2024–2025 scandal at Japan’s Fuji Television, in which a sexual assault allegation against celebrity host Nakai Masahiro exposed deep dysfunction in the broadcaster’s corporate culture and governance. It analyzes how the story – initially ignored by mainstream media – was broken by tabloid magazines and amplified by foreign press and social media, bypassing the gatekeeping mechanisms that normally protect powerful institutions in Japan. The article shows how Fuji TV’s attempts at public damage control backfired, triggering an unprecedented advertiser exodus, a damning third-party investigation, and lawsuits against former executives. It also reveals how the scandal laid bare the systemic exploitation of women in Japan’s broadcasting industry, sparking an online #MeToo movement in which women shared their own experiences of workplace harassment. The article asks whether this crisis marks a genuine turning point for accountability and gender equality in Japanese media, or whether it will fade as previous scandals have.

title: Staying vigilant during times of crisis: What shapes COVID-19 pandemic sensitivities?
abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Japan recorded comparatively favourable public-health outcomes while relying largely on voluntary citizen behaviour. Existing scholarship traces this pattern to communitarian norms and discipline, the prevalence of exclusionary and coercive social practices, and bottom-up enforcement of public-health recommendations driven by perceived undersecuritization. We approach the puzzle through the concept of vigilance, meaning the configurations of attention that operate alongside formal surveillance and function simultaneously as social control and community care, enabling responses to complex crises beyond the reach of state mandate. Drawing on twenty-two in-depth interviews, three years of (auto-)ethnographic fieldwork in Tokyo, and complementary analysis of policy and media texts (2020–2023), we trace how pandemic sensitivities were shaped by the everyday texture of urban life. Four interacting factors emerge as drivers of sensitisation and desensitisation: practical knowledge about risk, the rhythm of disruptions to daily routines, the diversification of pandemic narratives, and the materiality of risk in the environment. Each factor can intensify attention to threat or absorb it into the mundane. As an unusually rich empirical case, COVID-19 reveals how vigilance regimes are produced and dissolved through urban daily life. These insights can sharpen the governance of latent, protracted, and complex public emergencies.

title: Decentering digital humanities: a systematic review of research on Shakespeare digital archiving
abstract: Abstract Digital archives function as critical infrastructures for the preservation, circulation, and reinterpretation of Shakespearean texts and performances. Despite substantial practical development, the interdisciplinary research landscape of Shakespeare digital archiving has not yet been systematically synthesized. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses-guided systematic review is therefore conducted, drawing on thirty-two studies published between 1990 and 2025 in the Web of Science and Scopus databases. By integrating cross-analysis of thematic and methodological development, this review provides the first structured synthesis of the field’s evolution over thirty-five years. Although participation from non-Western regions has increased, institutional leadership and scholarly authority remain largely concentrated within Western academic contexts. Research themes have broadened from early technical implementation to include pedagogy and interculturality, but conventional infrastructural and editorial standards continue to shape practice. Methodologically, qualitative case-based inquiry persists as the dominant paradigm, while quantitative and user-centered approaches remain comparatively marginal. This review positions Shakespeare digital archiving as a critical site where technological standards and institutional authority intersect, contributing to broader debates in digital humanities regarding openness, participation, and …

title: What We Read while Looking Up from the Book: A Review of The Routledge Companion to Libraries, Archives, and the Digital Humanities
abstract: This review of The Routledge Companion to Libraries, Archives, and the Digital Humanities, edited by Isabel Galina Russell and Glen Layne-Worthey, highlights the book’s acute representation of the work performed by librarians, archivists and digital humanists. By means of the thoughtful selection and organization of more than thirty chapters, the editors show that libraries and archives are spaces that function because of the relations between five different systems: ethical-ideological, methodological, public, epistemological, and social. The review summarises each one of these systems and explains how they interact to showcase the complexities of academic practices such as digital preservation, digitisation, and text mining.

title: The (Im)possibility of Autonomous Feminist Infrastructures
abstract: Scaling-up, speeding-up, and powering-up of technology are all coterminous to the hegemonic cycle of infrastructural development. These capitalist impulses shrink the possibilities of building technology from critical perspectives. As such, this paper explores the (im)possibility—the possibility and impossibility—of autonomous feminist infrastructures. We focus specifically on feminist servers as a case study of these infrastructures, critically reflecting on our experimentation to build a prototype server. We contextualise this experiment with our work on Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities (DH), drawing a line from feminist histories in computing to development of feminist servers. Orienting our movement towards our own prototype server, we outline our theoretical framework of queer phenomenology. We expand on queer and feminist theorisation of infrastructure, outlining the relational role of infrastructure, in bridging and walling out communities. From our historical context and theoretical framing, we draw insights from experimentations. We outline the possibilities and negotiations with existing infrastructures in building autonomous feminist servers. Through our experimentation and reflections, we emphasise the need for a plurality of infrastructures and an exploration of the socio-technical entanglements in which such infrastructures exist.

title: Calabash Gourds in the Work of Roberto Evangelista: Amazonian Agencies and Trajectories
abstract: This paper addresses the use of calabash gourds by Brazilian artist Roberto Evangelista (1946–2019). I argue that an assessment of Evangelista’s work can lay the groundwork for reconceptualizing the Amazon basin as a historical landscape shaped by the trajectories and associations of human and more-than-human actors across temporal-geographical distances. This paper’s contribution is threefold: first, it delineates the Amazon’s insertion into global networks and its long-term participation in historical processes. Secondly, it emphasizes the relevance of Amazonian contemporary art for rethinking the Amazon beyond fixed geographical frontiers and modern ideas of pristine nature. Lastly, by adopting an object-based methodology and focusing on trajectories, this paper also makes an ecocritical contribution to the field of art history.
journal: H-ART Revista de historia teoría y crítica de arte

title: The plague of Egypt crossing the Red Sea: The arrival and focalisation of plague in the southern Red Sea region in the 1430s
abstract: Abstract Drawing on textual, archaeological, and palaeoclimatic evidence, this article reconstructs the broad patterns of plague’s arrival in the southern Red Sea region during the 1430s. It contends that this initial introduction led to the formation of a medium-term reservoir that generated recurrent epidemic waves over the subsequent 150–200 years. This development is attributed to the interplay of environmental and human-driven factors acting together. The study adopts a dual approach: first, it examines how commercial networks across the Red Sea facilitated the spread of the plague; second, it investigates the environmental and topographical shifts in the southern Red Sea between 1370 and 1470 to understand how these conditions allowed the disease to become endemic to the region.

title: Nakai Masakazu and the Revolutionary Potential of Consumption: From Bi-hihyō to the “Logic of the Committee” and Kyoto’s “Housing Problem” in 1930s Japan
abstract: Abstract This article focuses on the prewar theoretical and print activities of Kyoto school philosopher Nakai Masakazu. It spotlights Nakai’s efforts to confront alienation under finance capitalism and inspire a new “critical” and “cooperative” form of mass subjectivity in consumers. The article contributes to extant scholarship in two ways. First, it develops Nakai’s novel interpretation of Marxism and consumer struggle in connection with his mid-1930s article “Logic of the Committee” (“Iinkai no ronri”) and his work on the tabloid-format newspaper Doyōbi (Saturday). Second, it provides a broader picture of Nakai’s philosophical development by showing how these ideas trace back to his involvement with an understudied set of coterie journals from the early 1930s: Bi-hihyō (Aesthetics/Criticism) and Sekai bunka (World Culture). The article divides into three parts, each of which moves across theory and praxis. Part 1 focuses on Nakai’s work on Bi-hihyō and Sekai bunka. It traces the historical development of Nakai’s early philosophy of collectivity, media technology, and specialization and massification in connection with the “crisis” conditions of early 1930s Japan. Part 2 focuses on Nakai’s attempts to develop and consolidate these concepts in the context of finance capitalism in his seminal “Logic of the Committee.” In particular, it shows how Nakai reinterpreted these early philosophical concepts in terms of consumer alienation. Part 3 then focuses on Nakai’s response to …

title: Esperanto on the Radio: Broadcasting Infrastructure and the Politics of Universal Speech in the Japanese Empire
abstract: Abstract This article explores the interface between Esperanto and the radio in the Japanese Empire. Viewing radio as more than simply a mode of conveyance, it examines the tensions that emerged when a universalizing language met a universalizing medium. The following sections explore how new communication infrastructure enabled Esperantists’ claims to political salience. Radio in the Japanese empire helped articulate powerful forecasts of political solidarity, liberated from the restraints of space or state. However, Esperanto on the radio also appeared in ways that deepened the borders of colonial relations and linguistic hierarchies. The article first discusses the history of radio infrastructure in the Japanese Empire and its role in shaping linguistic topography of the 1920s and 1930s. It then turns to a case study of the 1928 “Esperanto Evening” broadcast from colonial Taiwan by Japanese Esperantists. As one of the few surviving examples of when universalizing language and media met, the transcript of this broadcast reveals the limits of Esperanto’s emancipatory reach.

title: The Neighborhood as Refuge: Dignity, Inclusiveness, and Compassion in Takeda Rintarō’s “Kamagasaki” (1933)
abstract: Abstract Kamagasaki, an urban enclave in Osaka, maintains a long history of marginalization that can be traced to the late 1890s. This article examines the representation of Kamagasaki in Osaka writer Takeda Rintarō’s novella “Kamagasaki.” Published in 1933, shortly after the economically prosperous “Greater Osaka” (“Dai Osaka”) period had ended, the story features the underclass and working-class people in the neighborhood of Kamagasaki, revealing how Osaka’s development has concealed issues, including economic exploitation and social division. This article introduces the concepts of “a compassionate participant” instead of adopting existing tropes of observers of city life, such as the flâneur and the “curiosity hunter” (ryōkisha). Through the perspective of such an observer, Takeda represents the issues of poverty, segregation, and homelessness in a humanistic manner. Simultaneously, by constructing various voices for fictional characters in the novella, Takeda highlights the importance of the “internal gaze” and voices from Kamagasaki. This article argues that by emphasizing how the locals value dignity and interpersonal bonds, Takeda’s representations of Kamagasaki subvert the stereotype of urban margins as morally degenerate. Through his conscious resistance to the social stigma imposed on Kamagasaki by dominant national discourse, which reduces Kamagasaki to a place of degeneration and danger, Takeda depicts a neighborhood characterized by shared attachment and …

title: Match me if you can: aligning historical posters and newspaper articles via multimodal deep learning
abstract: Abstract Multimodal deep learning (MDL) has potential for digital history (DH) research, from simple tasks such as image or text classification, to more sophisticated ones such as information retrieval (IR). We propose a novel IR method based on vision language models (VLMs), a class of MDL models, to extract embeddings from images and text to find connections among unrelated image and text datasets that are challenging to find using conventional approaches such as keyword search. We evaluate our method with a proof-of-concept case study on debates surrounding the civil usage of nuclear power in Europe, based on poster images from the Landelijk Kernenergie Archief website and German newspaper articles found in the Impresso corpus, where both datasets are assumed to share some common themes. We find that poster images and newspaper articles can be automatically matched from independent sources based on representations extracted by pre-trained VLMs. We further find that VLMs achieve better performance when translating newspaper articles to English or summarizing them in English. Ultimately, our work bridges the gap of cross-modal and cross-lingual IR for DH, showing real-world applicability of MDL and opening new avenues in DH research. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/StevenXuf/MatchMeIfYouCan.

title: Counting costs: the categorization of eighteenth-century theatrical expenditure for the Theatronomics database
abstract: Abstract The design and implementation of categories is an important part of digital humanities research, for which theoretical discussion is still relatively underdeveloped. This article presents an instructive case study from the Theatronomics project: the categorization of some 159,000 items of theatrical expenditure recorded 1732–1809. It explores the key considerations involved in categorizing financial data for a database; explains why the team adopted a pragmatic–explorative method, highly manual in nature; illustrates the major problems confronted during the process; and offers suggestions for further thinking on, and enacting of, digital humanities categorization. It advances three main arguments. First, categorization is not a ‘natural’ or ‘common-sense’ process. Scholars working on databases should consider the multiple different methods of categorization available, and the various and sometimes contradictory principles involved in categorization, before designing a method that aligns with their project’s aims, sources, and resources. Second, scholars should assess the uncertainty in their dataset, and consider how to represent it in their categorization model. Third, a model that involves multiple layers of categories can be effective in solving some of the key problems involved in categorization. This article also explains how Theatronomics’s expenses data, categorized in accordance with those three arguments, contributes to scholarship on Georgian theatre, …

title: The Dark Side of Ruins in Ancient Maya Living Landscapes
abstract: Abstract Ruination studies allow one to see the past not as a fixed “thing” but as living landscapes. Over the past two decades, Mesoamerican scholars have increasingly recognized that ruins were an integral part of ancient Mesoamerican peoples’ experiences in and with the world and not just a modern invention of cultural heritage. Any understanding of ancient Maya ruins must consider the Indigenous ontologies, cosmologies, and myths of peoples of that region. Indigenous approaches highlight the affective and dynamic nature of ruins, perspectives that can be put in conversation with metaphysical or posthumanist ideas more generally. One particularity of ruins in the Maya area is that they often were, and in many cases still are, entangled with forest beings that are both feared and revered. This article reviews some of the ways in which ancient Maya peoples lived with ruins, drawing a number of case examples from the Maya site of Ucanal in Petén, Guatemala, and then contextualizes these findings with the darker side of ruins. This darker side of ruins was part of the making of moral communities that were—and are—in a constant state of motion.

title: Reversing the history of philosophy
abstract: This article introduces a new teaching method for the history of philosophy that combines a reverse chronological approach with a critical analysis of the traditional canon. This approach aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the history of philosophy while challenging entrenched biases, such as androcentrism and eurocentrism. By starting with contemporary issues and working backwards in time this reverse chronological approach enacts a radical shift in perspective, aiming to provide a more nuanced and representative picture of the history of philosophy and challenging the canon as a normative standard. This new method prioritizes reception over influence and promotes a broader and more inclusive understanding of the discipline. Rather than seeking to preserve a patriarchal and parochial definition of philosophy, this approach aims to foster an ongoing critical engagement with both the history and historiography of philosophy. A key pedagogical advantage is its relatability, starting with contemporary issues to activate students and highlight the relevance of historical inquiry to current debates.

title: Eingegangene Bücher
Die „Zeit“ der Demokratie. Zeitstrukturen und temporale Diskurse in der parlamentarischen Praxis der Bundesrepublik
abstract: Zusammenfassung Der Aufsatz analysiert die Bedeutung von Zeit für die Geschichte moderner Demokratien. Er argumentiert, dass Zeitstrukturen und Zeitdiskurse eine prägende, in der Forschung bislang jedoch weitgehend übersehene Dimension der parlamentarischen Praxis darstellen. Im ersten Teil wird ein Analyserahmen entwickelt, der fünf Zeitdimensionen unterscheidet: als Horizont, Struktur, Ressource, Diskurs und Gegenstand. Der zweite Teil untersucht am Beispiel der Bundesrepublik, auf welche Weise Fragen von Zeit und Zeitlichkeit demokratische Strukturen und Praktiken beeinflussten – etwa in den Debatten über die parlamentarische Geschäftsordnung und deren Reformen, in parlamentarischen Auseinandersetzungen über konkrete Gesetzesvorhaben sowie im Zusammenspiel zwischen Parlament, Medien und Öffentlichkeit.

Vom Semitismus zum Antisemitismus? Die Kategorie des Semitischen in den Wissenschaften des 19. Jahrhunderts und ihr Beitrag zur Judenfeindschaft
abstract: Zusammenfassung Über die etymologische Sinnlosigkeit des Begriffs „Antisemitismus“ ist sich die Antisemitismusforschung weithin einig: Der am Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts zunächst als Selbstbezeichnung der Antisemiten aufkommende Begriff bezog sich niemals auf eine Ablehnung der „Semiten“, sondern ausschließlich auf Juden und Judentum und hat sich seither als Synonym für die (moderne) Judenfeindschaft etabliert. Der begriffliche Rückgriff auf den „Semitismus“ wird dabei zumeist mit einer negativen Konnotation der sogenannten Semiten im (wissenschaftlichen) Diskurs des 19. Jahrhunderts erklärt. Die Entstehungs- und Verwendungsgeschichte der Kategorie des Semitischen zeigt jedoch ein deutlich komplexeres Bild: Wie im Folgenden anhand einer Untersuchung von Publikationen aus den zeitgenössischen Sprach-, Orient- und Bibelwissenschaften gezeigt wird, bestand zwischen abwertenden Darstellungen der sogenannten Semiten und antisemitischen Positionierungen kein direkter Zusammenhang – ebenso wenig wie zwischen romantisierenden Darstellungen und einer Ablehnung des Antisemitismus. Vor diesem Hintergrund vermögen auch jüngere Vorschläge nicht zu überzeugen, den Begriff „Antisemitismus“ wörtlich zu lesen und auf einen zusammenhängenden Abwertungsdiskurs gegenüber Juden und Arabern (bzw. Judentum und Islam) im 19. Jahrhundert zu schließen.

Industrial Lessons Abroad: Chinese Engineers in Britain, 1933–1948
abstract: Abstract: This article explores the dynamic development of the Federation of British Industries Chinese Apprenticeships Scheme from 1933 to 1948, examining how China’s national reconstruction agenda intersected with Britain’s trade-political interests in technology and engineering. It argues that the scheme embodies key features of Sino-British educational, scientific, and cultural initiatives in the 1930s and 1940s—advancing cultural diplomacy while steering China toward purchasing relationships favorable to Britain. Adopting a multi-perspective approach that combines institutional analysis and bio-graphical research, the article moves beyond traditional narratives of modernization, patriotism, and Sino-British friendship to uncover key tensions within this transnational, factory-based initiative, including international competition in foreign manufacturing exports, the mismatch between Chinese engineering graduates and Britain’s apprenticeship system, Britain’s chronic under-resourcing in cultural diplomacy, and Chinese engineers’ frustrations under nationalist statism. It offers insights into Britain’s cultural diplomacy, China’s nation-building efforts, and broader Sino-British trade and cultural exchanges in the twentieth century.

Anti-Colonial Activism and Multi-Imperial Entanglements: Reassessing the 1932 Hongkou Bombing Incident in Interwar Shanghai
abstract: Abstract: This article examines the 1932 Hongkou Park Bombing Incident in Shanghai as a critical episode of anti-colonial resistance that reveals the entangled dynamics of empire, nationalism, and global political activism in the interwar period. Despite its historical significance, the incident remains relatively under-studied in English-language scholarship. This article addresses that gap by situating the bombing within the distinctive urban setting of interwar Shanghai. Drawing on multilingual archival sources and press coverage, this study shows how the bombing incident catalyzed a range of responses: it exposed the contra-dictions of British imperial strategy, prompted Franco-Japanese collaboration in colonial policing, and deepened covert support from the Chinese Nationalist Government. This article argues that the Hongkou Incident not only brought into sharp relief existing power differentials but also served as a catalyst for renegotiating power relations and modes of interaction among agents of multiple empires and local Chinese authorities in the city of Shanghai. In doing so, it contributes to global historiographies of anti-colonialism by demonstrating how interwar Shanghai functioned not only as a site of colonial governance and repression but also as a crucible of trans-Asian political mobilization and media discourse.

title: Kita Ikki and Zeng Qi: National Socialism in East Asia, Late 1910s–Early 1930s
abstract: Abstract: This article explores emergent radical political discourse in East Asia driven, at least partially, by regionalized national socialism, which was one of the two most influential revolutionary ideologies, alongside communism, in the early twentieth-century world. Despite a wealth of scholarship about national struggles and communist movements in the political radicalization of East Asia from the late 1910s to the early 1930s, it is still difficult to understand the role national socialism played in this radicalization, as seen in the ascendance of Kita Ikki and Zeng Qi, the two leading national socialists in Japan and China in this era. By comparing Kita’s and Zeng’s transformative ideas, this article documents radical discursive changes.

abstract: Abstract: This article analyzes the importance of Korean skilled workers in Japan during and after the East Asian War of 1592–1598. By tracing the story of the Korean Pak Hoin and his descendants, this article demonstrates the close relationship between domains and migrants. In doing so, it demonstrates that migrants were not only widespread throughout early Tokugawa Japan, but also that their experiences were highly varied. By placing Hoin’s experience next to that of other Korean migrants, this article identifies some of the factors that influenced migrant experiences and the varying impact they had on their local environments.

The Spanish Naval Station in the Pacific: A Frustrated Project of Global Regeneration (1833–1866)
abstract: Abstract: The project to install a permanent naval station on the South American shores of the Pacific attracted the consensus of Spain’s political-intellectual, military, and diplomatic elites during the reign of Isabel II (1844–1868). This article reconstructs the constellation of strategic, economic, legal, and political arguments used by the Spanish monarchy’s diplomatic agents to support the need to station warships in its former Pacific dominions. It also identifies these agents’ socioeconomic coordinates, networks, and interests, evaluating the factual consequences of their attempts to create the station. We will argue that Spanish political elites conceived the naval station as a critical element in the new repertoire of instruments of power necessary for configuring a “second Spanish empire” based on the ideological postulates of navalism, pan-Hispanism, and the imperialism of free trade. This case study allows us to make some theoretical contributions to understanding the crucial functions that naval stations performed as elements of imperial power in the nineteenth century.

abstract: In 1839, Léonie d’Aunet (1820–79) became the first European woman to take part in a scientific expedition to Spitsbergen. In her first essay Voyage d’une femme au Spitzberg (1854), she documents Arctic landscapes, fauna, and social environments she encountered, offering one of the earliest examples of what could be read today as affective and situated ethnography, grounded in her attentive observation of both living beings and human worlds. Her writing combines precise description, humour, and intimacy, thus providing a new perspective on travel writing, offering an alternative to the heroic and extractive narratives that shaped nineteenth-century exploration. Her descriptions of seabirds and of the conditions of travelling as a woman reveal an attention to the living world, positioning her as a precursor to later feminist and ecological perspectives. The episode describing the transformation of the captain’s cabin into a “nest” on board La Recherche illustrates the sensitive dimension of her experience within a male-dominated environment. This detail inspired the author’s artistic practice, whose work revisits d’Aunet’s legacy through performative methods. Making kinship with plants and the multiple meanings of care in Amazonian Indigenous gardens
abstract: This paper focuses on the bonds of kinship and care between humans, cultivated plants, and other-than-human beings in Indigenous gardens, myths, rituals, and shamanism, across Lowland South America. Drawing on Krahô ethnography and a review of ethnological literature, it highlights the contributions of Americanist ethnology to wider debates about multispecies relation, particularly with regard to vegetal agency. By exploring the ambivalent meanings of care- such as “caring,” “raising,” and “nurturing,” as well as “being careful,” “having respect,” and “taking precautions”- I examine how kinship relations between humans and their cultivated plants are made through care and unmade through its absence (which may point to dehumanization and transformation of person). I argue that the vitality, abundance, and diversity of gardens emerge through relations of interdependence, bodily co-constitution, and reciprocity among humans, plants, spirits, and cosmological “owners,” also considering the dangers of daily life and relationships of counter-predation. I also suggest that vegetal regeneration is significant for understanding processes of kinship, its continuity, transformation, and renewal in Indigenous worlds, offering a broader perspective on the intertwined life cycles of humans and plants.
journal: Tipití Journal of the Society for the Anthropology of Lowland South America

title: Good Women, Mediocre Men: Hierarchy in Narrative and Digital Prosopography
abstract: Creating a prosopography of people who engaged with the Georgian theatre requires interrogating mixed media sources, including archival documents; print materials including anecdotal magazine articles, playbills, and biographies; digital authority records like those compiled by the Virtual International Authority File (VIAF); other databases; and traditional scholarship about theatre history. Embedded within this ecosystem of sources is a hierarchy of information which often privileges the cultural capital that comes with celebrity and notoriety. In this article, we use the careers of the actor Alexander Pope and his two wives, Elizabeth Younge and Maria Ann Campion, as case studies to investigate how these hierarchies are inscribed and reinscribed first in historical documents and subsequently in modern scholarship. In a period with five prominent theatrical Popes, we argue for digital prosopography as a methodology that can counter these hierarchies. When incorporated into a project like ‘Theatronomics: The Business of Theatre, 1732-1809’, which links people to their earnings and their box office power, digital prosopography enables us to illuminate the labour of individuals that might otherwise be concealed by the mythos of celebrity, and the institution of the theatre more generally.

title: Animals, Gaúchos and Drovers in the Historical Formation of Southern Brazil (XVI–XIX Centuries)
abstract: The objective of this article is to provide an account of the importance of cattle, horses and mules to the historical and socioeconomic formation of Southern Brazil and Rio Grande do Sul, paying more attention than the traditional narratives to explaining the violence against these animals, in what can be called a vegan approach. The formation and transformation of gaúcho identity in relation to their treatment of animals is also addressed. The natural environment of the Pampas grasslands is highlighted as facilitator to the dissemination of these animals by Europeans and their quick multiplication. This, in turn, collaborated with the drovers, the dried beef industry, militarism and the culture of violence against animals and people in this region of frontier between the Portuguese and the Spanish Empires. This article was published open access under a CC BY licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

title: Listening to Deep Time: Nineteenth-Century Reconstructions of Carboniferous Soundscapes
abstract: This article investigates how nineteenth-century British writers imagined the soundscapes of ancient environments, focusing on the Carboniferous period as a case study. Often framed as the geological era that birthed coal – and by extension, industrial modernity – the Carboniferous served as fertile ground for textual reconstructions of prehistoric environments. While such reconstructions have traditionally privileged the visual, this study foregrounds the auditory, analysing depictions of silence, vegetal rustling and insect sounds in both scientific and popular Victorian writing. Methodologically, the article draws on concepts from sound studies to integrate the auditory into environmental history – proposing ‘Carboniferous silence’ as a rhetorical tool for evoking absence, estrangement and deep temporal distance. Tracing the shift from imagined stillness to the post-1860s integration of fossil-based insect acoustics, it argues that soundscapes functioned as affective and epistemological bridges between the primeval past and the industrial present.
